title: Skyr vs. cottage cheese: protein and calories

seo.title: Skyr vs. cottage cheese: equal-serving comparison
seo.meta_description: Compare 150 g servings of plain skyr and 2% cottage cheese for protein, calories, fat, calcium and sodium.
seo.search_intent: Compare skyr and cottage cheese for protein and calories

excerpt: In equal 150 g servings, current labels are surprisingly close for energy: Icelandic Provisions Plain Skyr has 120 calories and 17 g protein; Good Culture 2% cottage cheese has 130 calories and 19 g protein. The bigger contrast is sodium: 55 mg in skyr versus 520 mg in cottage cheese.
content_html:
Skyr and cottage cheese are both popular high-protein dairy foods, and this is one comparison where package sizes make an unusually clean side-by-side possible: both current single servings can be compared at 150 g.

Equal 150 g servings

Plain skyr2% cottage cheese
Calories120130
Protein17 g19 g
Fat2.5 g3 g
Total sugars3 g5 g
Sodium55 mg520 mg

Cottage cheese provides 2 g more protein for only 10 extra calories in these products.

The largest nutritional difference is sodium

Cottage cheese is salted. The Good Culture serving has 520 mg sodium, almost ten times the 55 mg in the skyr cup. That does not make cottage cheese a poor food, but it is a meaningful difference for someone tracking sodium.

Calcium is not identical either

The skyr lists 190 mg calcium per 150 g; the cottage cheese lists 140 mg. Both contribute calcium, but product-to-product variation is real.

A serving reveals two fairly similar protein foods

At the same 150 g serving, skyr and cottage cheese can come quite close in protein and calories, so the decision no longer depends on a one- or two-gram difference. The more practical contrast is often sodium, texture and use: skyr behaves like a thick yogurt, while cottage cheese is a fresh curd cheese.

That is also why protein per 100 g does not tell the whole story. A food that fits your breakfast, lunch or snack more naturally can be the more useful choice even if it loses by a tiny amount in the table.

Texture and meal use

Skyr is smooth and yogurt-like. Cottage cheese has distinct curds and a savory, saltier profile, making it easy to use in toast, eggs, salads or pasta fillings.

For maximum protein, cottage wins narrowly here; for much lower sodium, skyr wins decisively.

Protein numbers depend heavily on the specific product

Plain skyr is typically strained and therefore protein-dense, while cottage cheese contains curds suspended in a creamy dressing. Both can reach impressive protein levels, but labels vary with fat percentage, moisture, and serving size. A single-serve skyr cup may contain roughly the same protein as a half cup of cottage cheese even though the weights differ. Comparing grams of protein per serving and per 100 calories is more useful than assuming one category always wins.

Flavored skyr can also contain considerable added sugar, while cottage cheese is often more notable for sodium. Those differences can outweigh a small protein advantage. Plain versions make the nutritional contrast easier to see and allow sweetness or seasoning to be added at home.

Texture and meal role can determine which one is more useful

Skyr has a smooth, tangy texture that fits breakfast bowls, fruit, oats, sauces, and desserts. Cottage cheese is chunkier and more savory, though it also works with fruit. It can be used on toast, in salads, baked dishes, or as a high-protein snack. A food that fits naturally into meals is more likely to be eaten consistently, so convenience and preference matter alongside the nutrient table.

Both foods can be filling because protein slows digestion compared with a low-protein snack. Full-fat versions may add more calories and satiety, while low-fat or fat-free versions can raise protein per calorie. Neither option is inherently best for everyone; energy needs, taste, and the rest of the meal determine the better fit.

Calcium, sodium, cultures, and lactose add nuance

Dairy products contribute calcium, phosphorus, vitamin B12, and high-quality protein, but exact amounts vary. Skyr often contains live cultures because it is cultured like yogurt, whereas cottage cheese may or may not contain live active cultures depending on processing. Cottage cheese commonly contains more sodium, so people watching sodium should compare labels rather than relying on category averages.

Lactose tolerance is individual. Strained cultured products such as skyr may be easier for some people to tolerate than milk, but they are not automatically lactose-free. Some cottage cheeses are available in lactose-free versions as well. If digestion is the deciding issue, the specific label and personal response matter more than the general name of the product.

For people using these foods after exercise, total protein across the day matters more than choosing the product with the highest single serving. Both provide complete dairy protein with essential amino acids, including leucine. A serving paired with fruit, oats, bread, or potatoes can contribute both protein and carbohydrate after training. Athletes with high energy needs may prefer a larger or higher-fat portion than someone choosing a lighter snack.

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: The cottage cheese example: 19 g versus 17 g in equal 150 g servings.

faq.question: Which has fewer calories?
faq.answer: Skyr by a small margin: 120 versus 130 calories.

faq.question: Which has more sodium?
faq.answer: Cottage cheese: 520 mg versus 55 mg per 150 g.

faq.question: Which has more calcium?
faq.answer: In these labels, skyr: 190 mg versus 140 mg in cottage cheese.
